changes.text: New: holzkube-managerd break-glass prints a short-lived admin token on the machine itself, for the case where the only way in is the machine. It grants nothing new — whoever can open the data directory already holds everything in it — so what it adds is a supported and audited way to use that, instead of hand-editing the store.

That token expires: fifteen minutes by default, a day at the very most. An ordinary service account still never expires, because an expiry nobody is awake to renew is an outage rather than a safeguard.

It is always the one account named break-glass, visible in every list, and minting again rotates it rather than leaving admin accounts nobody remembers creating. The act is written to the audit archive with the local user's name, before it happens and again with its outcome.
No HTTP route carries it, and a test keeps one from appearing: the reasoning above holds only for a subcommand operating on a path.

The wall has been redesigned after looking at how the boards that do this for a living are built — Grafana's own Kubernetes dashboards, the kube-mixin boards, polystat. It is split now: the left half answers "is anything wrong" from ten metres, the right half answers "what, and why" from one.

Its colours are solid fills rather than fifteen-per-cent tints. A tint is legible on a laptop at arm's length and gone at four metres on a television in a lit room, which is the only place this screen is ever read.

The 132 anonymous squares are one tile per namespace, each carrying the worst thing inside it by name — "postgres · 2 of 3 ready". Nothing is hidden by the roll-up: every tile shows its own count, the counts add up to the total, and anything not running is still named in full on the left.
The nodes are always named on the wall, not only once one has failed.
The headline is nine per cent of the screen's height, and says how many workloads and nodes it is talking about — "everything is running" means more when everything is 132 things.
A warning on the wall said when it last happened as a raw timestamp — "2026-09-20T09:58:00Z", on a television. It says "3 h ago" now.
On a phone the wall rendered completely and at about five pixels: its type is sized for a television, in units that shrink with the screen. It now has phone-sized type below tablet width.

On a phone the wall ran a third of its width off the right edge — names and warnings with it — and the layout guard had reported it as fine five runs in a row, because it forgives anything inside something that scrolls sideways. It no longer forgives a full-screen pane, and it now names what is sticking out.

A warning on the wall said "Failed Pod/dupl-test" and nothing about WHY. The cluster's own sentence — the only part of a warning with any content in it — was being fetched, carried through the API and then not drawn. It is on the screen now.
On a phone the wall had a black gap between the tiles and the footer, so scrolling down landed in nothing. The layout fills a fixed screen only where it cannot scroll.
The wall spells out what a square is: one workload — a deployment, statefulset, daemonset, job or cronjob — and not a single pod.

The wall hid everything that was working. Past sixty tiles it drew only the ones that were NOT fine — so on a cluster where everything runs it said "showing 0 of 132" and showed a black screen. It is two zones now: whatever needs attention is named and large at the top, and everything healthy is a dense field of colour grouped by namespace. Nothing is hidden, ever.

The screen says what a square is — "130 workloads, one square each" — with a key to the colours actually on it. You should not have to ask a wall what it means, and an answer given anywhere but on the wall is one nobody walking past ever gets.

It fills the screen now: three nodes are three wide tiles whose names fit rather than three narrow ones beside empty space, and the squares are as large as the room allows. On a phone the page scrolls instead of silently cutting off what does not fit.

The wall can be left up now. Make a link under Settings, open it on the screen once and bookmark it: it does not expire, so the screen keeps answering long after a session would have run out — and it is revoked from the same place when the screen comes down.

The link opens the wall and nothing else. Not a role and not a session: one named route accepts it, which you can check by reading the route table. It reads, it can never change anything, and it cannot see the audit archive, a Secret’s key names or a cluster’s configuration.

It is shown once — only its hash is kept — and it needs a label, because the question a revocation asks is which screen this was. The list says when each link was last used, which answers the other one: is it still on a wall?

A screen for the IT office. /wall shows every node and every workload as a tile, how full the cluster is, and the most recent warnings — no navigation, nothing to click, and it never scrolls: the tiles shrink to fit, and past a screenful it says how many there are and draws the ones that are not fine.

It says how old its answer is at all times, and dims when that answer is more than a few refreshes old. A wall that cannot go stale lies during exactly the incident it exists for. A failed refresh keeps the last answer up with its age showing rather than blanking the screen.

Five colours, not two: a CronJob between runs is not an outage, something you stopped on purpose is not broken, and a node nobody is hearing from is never green. Those three are what a red-and-green wall gets wrong, and the last one is the case the screen exists for.
It still needs somebody to sign in on it once, and a session expires — so it is not yet a screen to leave up for weeks. A long-lived, read-only, revocable kiosk link is the next piece.

The notice after signing in again at your identity provider is a window in the middle of the screen now, over a blurred page, so it cannot be scrolled past — and it is named after the action it is about. It used to read "and This destructive action has not run yet", because the action names are sentences of their own and no sentence around them reads correctly for all of them.
Forgetting, rebooting, shutting down or resetting a machine, and forgetting a cluster, are now named in the confirmation instead of all being "this destructive action".

On an address that only accepts single sign-on, the sign-in page now links to the address where the local account still works. It is derived from the addresses this instance answers to rather than configured, and if there is no honest answer it says the sentence without a link rather than guessing one.

After signing in again at your identity provider to confirm something destructive, the banner now RUNS it. One press, named after what you asked for. Before, it told you the action had not run and offered you a way back to the page, which reads as failure — and the journal shows exactly that: the window opened correctly, and nobody ever tried a second time. An action whose request carries a body still asks you to repeat it yourself, because carrying that across would mean storing it in the browser, and for the password change that body is the password.

Every single-replica database was marked as a problem for allowing no disruption — which is simply what a budget says when there is one copy of something. Six of them filled the Config page and pushed the ConfigMaps and Ingresses it exists for below them. A budget is now judged on whether it is MET; a pod already missing is the finding. What a drain would do to a single copy is still said on the row, because somebody about to drain a node needs to know it — said, not flagged.

The Kubernetes page showed a screenful of errors instead of a page on a cluster whose namespaces have no resource quota. An empty list was being answered as null, and the browser reads null and "missing" differently — so a page that had been tested, fixtured and released showed nothing at all. Every list in every Kubernetes answer is now an empty list when it is empty, a check walks all of them against a cluster with nothing in it, and the browser treats a null list as an empty one so this can never blank a page again.

The Kubernetes screen is ten pages instead of one. It had grown to fifteen cards on a single page — everything was reachable and nothing was findable. Overview, Workloads, Pods, Storage, Network, Config, Namespaces, Access, Events and Maintenance each have their own address now, so a link to one is a link you can send, the back button does what it looks like, and a page that fails takes only itself down.

The cluster and namespace you picked live in the address, so moving between those pages keeps them — and a link carries them with it. Picking a namespace now narrows every page rather than just the pod list.

How full the cluster is, on all three levels: the totals, each node, and what each pod reserved. This is the figure every cluster has — allocatable against what the pods REQUESTED — which is the scheduler's own arithmetic and therefore what decides whether the next pod starts. It sits beside the usage panel and neither is called the other: 90% requested at 5% used is over-reserved and will refuse work it could do, 20% requested at 95% used is about to fall over while looking empty.

Stop and start a service. "Stop this pod" is not something Kubernetes has — delete one and its controller makes another within seconds — so the controller is what stops. The replica count is written onto the workload before it goes to zero, and the screen tells you what a start will bring back before you press it: a three-replica service comes back as three, not silently as one.

A button for clearing out what is finished. It does not delete: it shows the list first, with a reason on every row, and only a second press removes exactly that list. Left alone are anything still running, the newest rollout of a deployment (the way back), a Job its CronJob still owns, and anything under an hour old. Images are not in the list and cannot be — Talos has no delete for them, the kubelet removes them itself when its disk fills, and the screen says so instead of offering a button that would do nothing.

A storage screen that answers what a claim list cannot: whether deleting destroys the data or keeps it, which pods mount a claim, whether it can be grown, and why a Pending claim is pending — two of the three causes are not faults at all. And volumes whose claim is gone while the data is still on the disk, which are invisible everywhere else and are either wasted space or exactly what you want back.

A networking screen built around the commonest broken thing in Kubernetes: a Service with nothing behind it, which looks completely healthy in every list while refusing every connection. Both endpoint counts are shown, because an unready endpoint is not in the load balancer at all. The namespaces with no NetworkPolicy are listed by name — they accept traffic from every pod in the cluster, which is Kubernetes's default rather than a setting anybody chose.

Who may do what. Who is an administrator is not a field in Kubernetes: it is worked out from the rules, so a hand-written role with wildcard verbs on wildcard resources counts whatever it is called. Bindings that grant nothing are marked — one naming a role that does not exist, or a service account that was never created, looks exactly like one that works, because RBAC checks neither.

Namespaces with what constrains them. A namespace stuck Terminating now says what is holding it, not just that it is stuck. A full quota is named as the reason the next pod is refused — that refusal lands on the pod as "exceeded quota" and nothing showed you the quota. And a compute quota with no LimitRange, which refuses every pod that sets no requests while the error blames the pod.

The kinds your cluster defines itself, since that is where its operators keep their state. One the API server is not serving is marked: every manifest naming it is refused, and nothing else in a cluster tells you.

A guard of our own turned out to be measuring a seventeen-hour-old build and passing every time — four new panels, unchanged numbers, exit 0. It builds what it measures now, and a failed build stops it rather than falling back.

Every workload kind is listed now, not only Deployments — StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs too. Your storage layer is a DaemonSet and your backup is a CronJob, and a list without them showed a cluster nobody runs. What each kind cannot do is not offered: a DaemonSet has no replica field, because its size is how many nodes match.

Beside them: ConfigMaps, Secrets, persistent volume claims, Ingresses, autoscalers and disruption budgets. Each answers something the workload list cannot — where the setting lives, whether a URL reaches the cluster, why a claim is Pending, why a replica count goes back after you scale by hand, why a drain refuses. Whatever is the reason something is stuck comes first.
Secrets are listed and never read: the names and key names answer "does this namespace have the pull secret", and no value appears anywhere. Base64 is not encryption.

Objects can be removed, one at a time, by typing the name back. There is no delete-all and no label selector, and deleting a Namespace is refused: it removes everything inside it and nothing stops it once it starts.

Every node has a "Why?" button for the question a pod cannot answer. Taints in words — NoExecute evicts what is already there, NoSchedule only keeps new pods off. Conditions with the inversion handled. And how much room the scheduler has left, which is what pods REQUESTED rather than what they use: a node at 5% CPU can still be full.
If you install metrics-server, usage appears beside it. Without one the screen says nobody is collecting this, which is not the same as zero — Talos does not ship one.

A command can be run in a container, and it is deliberately not a terminal: a program and its arguments run once and the output comes back. A shell with a string is refused, because an archive that recorded "sh -lc" could not say what happened. It runs under your identity or not at all. There is no port-forward: that would mean this daemon holding a listener with nobody's authentication behind it.

Your cluster's own audit log can now name the person instead of this product. Tell holzkube-manager the name your API server knows you by, and every Kubernetes request carries it: the API server records both — this product as the impersonator, you as the actor — and your cluster's RBAC decides what you may do.

Nothing is stored before your cluster has been asked. The panel runs an access review for every permission this product issues, as that identity, and shows your cluster's own verdicts and reasons. A name your RBAC has never heard of would otherwise break every Kubernetes screen at once and look like the product is broken rather than a setting being wrong.

A refusal is never retried as the administrator. That rule is what makes this worth having: with a fallback every request would succeed either way, your RBAC would decide nothing, and your audit log would show an administrator action whenever somebody lacked a role.
One button goes back to this product's own certificate, so a wrong name is a minute rather than an afternoon.
Until you set it, nothing changes: requests keep arriving as holzkube-manager in system:masters, and the screen says plainly what that costs you.
The Kubernetes screen now answers why something is broken, not only that it is. Every pod has a "Why?" button: which container failed, how it ended, its log, and what the cluster reported about it.

Logs, and by default the log of the run that ALREADY CRASHED. A pod in CrashLoopBackOff has printed nothing in its current container — everything that explains the crash belongs to the run that ended, and a log view without that answers every crash loop with an empty box.

Container detail says how a run ended in words: exit code 137 is a memory limit, ImagePullBackOff never started, and a container that asked for no CPU or memory is named as one the scheduler places blind.

Events, per pod and for the whole cluster, with warnings first. "Pending" is never explained by the pod — it is explained by "0/2 nodes are available: insufficient cpu", which exists only here. An empty list always says why it is not a claim that nothing happened: a cluster forgets its events after about an hour.

Any object can be shown as YAML, for the question the lists do not cover — a toleration, a node selector, somebody's controller annotation. A Secret is refused rather than redacted: its data is base64, not encryption, and a redaction that misses one field puts a credential on a screen that promised it would not.

None of a log's content is archived. A log line is whatever the workload printed, the audit archive is kept forever, and a secret written there has no path that removes it. The archive records that somebody read the log of a named pod.

The node detail page is usable on a phone. Fifteen of its values ran off the right edge with no way to scroll them back — the processor line, the memory, the disks and the network interfaces — because the label column could not shrink. Labels and values stack on a phone now, and long values wrap.

The same pattern was corrected in four more places that had not shown themselves yet: the cluster cards, the job cards, the cluster templates and the configuration screen. They were getting away with it only because their values are shorter.

The layout guard had been checking eleven screens out of fourteen. It now also drives the node detail page and — in the only order that makes them measurable — the sign-in and first-run screens, which are the first two anybody ever sees.

The whole interface now works on a phone. Below a tablet's width a table is no longer a table: rows you act on — nodes, pods, deployments, clusters, accounts — become cards with the name on top, the figures labelled, and the buttons underneath the name they act on. Rows you scan — the audit archive, recent activity, saved schematics — become a compact list, and tapping one opens its detail.

The reason is not appearance. A wide table on a phone scrolls sideways, and the first column is what disappears first: you end up looking at a "Scale" field and a "Roll pods" button with no way to tell which deployment they would act on. An action detached from its subject is a different and worse problem than an ugly screen, and that is what this removes.
Every control you tap is at least 44px on a phone. Ten were smaller — the node links, the cluster links, and the "Download a talosconfig" line and its neighbours, which were 20px tall.

This is measured rather than hoped for. The layout guard drives every screen at phone and desk width in a real browser and fails the build on three things: an element past the right edge with nothing to scroll, a control under 44px, and a table wider than the screen. The third is new.

The guard itself had been passing for the wrong reason: it started with an empty data directory, so every screen that shows rows showed none. It renders real rows now — with deliberately long names, because short ones measure a layout nobody has. The first run with data found eight tables between 521 and 1027 pixels wide and ten controls too small to hit, all of which had been passing for as long as the guard existed.

holzkube-manager can now manage Kubernetes and not only watch it. Cordon a node so nothing new is scheduled onto it, drain one so its pods move, restart a pod, scale a deployment, roll its pods, apply a manifest, and read a health or metrics endpoint from a service. Until now two screens told you to cordon and drain by hand first, because there was no Kubernetes client to do it with.

A drain evicts rather than deletes, so a PodDisruptionBudget can refuse it — and when one does, the answer names the pod and the budget instead of pushing past it. Two decisions stay yours, the same two kubectl refuses to take: a pod nothing owns is gone rather than moved once it is evicted, and a pod with local storage loses that storage when it moves.

"Restart this pod" is refused when nothing owns it. Kubernetes has no restart verb — it has "delete the pod and let the controller make another" — and those are the same operation only while a controller exists. Deleting a bare pod because somebody clicked a word would destroy something on the strength of that word.

Scaling and rolling are kept apart, because they are not the same thing. Scaling changes how many pods there are; a rollout restart replaces the pods there are under the deployment's own surge, maxUnavailable and readiness probes, so the workload stays up. Deleting a deployment's pods one at a time would take it down.

Manifests: paste one, press Plan, read what it would do, then Apply. Whether each object is created or updated comes from asking your cluster — a manifest looks identical either way — and Apply stays disabled until a plan exists for exactly the text in the box. Editing throws the plan away, because a plan for a document you have since changed is worse than none.

An apply never forces. When another field manager owns a field your manifest sets, the API server says so and this reports it instead of winning: forcing takes the value away from whatever is managing it, and that thing will set it back. Every object is attempted and each failure carries its reason, so an apply where the sixth of ten conflicts tells you which nine went through. Nothing is ever deleted — there is no prune.

Reach a service: pick a port, type a path, read the answer as text. It fetches; it does not host. A workload's own content type is deliberately thrown away, because rendering a pod's markup here would put it in the origin holding your session — any pod in the cluster could then script this interface. Only GET is ever sent, and it goes through the API server's own proxy rather than a tunnel this daemon opens.

Fixed before you could see it: client-go throttles itself to five requests a second, and a manifest plan asks your cluster about every object. Sixty objects took ten seconds of queueing inside this process — after which the screen would have blamed your cluster for being slow. Measured, raised to kubectl's own limits, and held by a test that fails at exactly the old number.

Said plainly rather than left out: neither manifests nor the service proxy has ever run against a real cluster. Every part is measured against a simulated API server this repository ships, which serves real Kubernetes JSON over real TLS with a real client certificate — but it has no admission webhooks and no managed-fields bookkeeping. The mechanism and the refusals are proven; your cluster's reaction to your manifest is not.

holzkube-manager now talks to Kubernetes itself. A new screen shows what the cluster's own API server says: its nodes as Kubernetes sees them — registered, ready, cordoned — and its pods, filtered by namespace. This is allowed to disagree with the Nodes screen, which reads the machine API, and where the two differ that difference is the answer you came for.

A pod shows its phase and its readiness, not one of the two. "Running" with 1 of 2 containers ready is a workload that does not work, and a screen that showed only the phase would call it healthy. Restart counts and the container's own reason — CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff — are there for the same purpose.

It uses a certificate it issues itself, from the Kubernetes authority it already holds for each adopted cluster, valid for an hour and never written to disk. It introduces itself as holzkube-manager rather than as admin, so your cluster's own audit log records who acted.

An API server that does not answer is not a cluster with nothing running. The screen says it was asked and did not answer instead of showing an empty list — the same rule the node list already follows.

Where the API server is comes from the cluster, not from arithmetic: it is read out of a control-plane node's own configuration. Since Talos 1.14 that address lives in a document of its own, and a version of this that read only the documented place would never have reached this cluster at all.

Forgetting a cluster no longer fails with a message about a revision. The machines of that cluster are being watched the whole time, and a health check landing in the same instant made the write collide with itself — you would have seen an error you cannot act on, and the cluster still there. It now retries and keeps whatever the health check just recorded.

The checks that ask whether the Image Factory still answers the way this build expects now run every week on their own. They existed and nothing ever started them, so their silence meant nothing. The first real run says the recordings still match.

A cluster's Talos certificate authority can be rotated. This is the operation the product has been saying it does not do, and it is the widest silent damage radius in it: rotating changes what every node trusts. It runs as a job in four passes — every node accepts the new authority, every node starts issuing from it, holzkube-manager takes a certificate from it and proves it against a node, and only then does the old one stop being accepted. Between the passes the cluster trusts two authorities, which is a working state, so an interrupted rotation is continued rather than restarted.

It refuses unless every node answers, and it checks that after the first pass rather than at the start — the last moment where stopping costs nothing. A node that misses the first pass refuses the certificate every other node accepts after the second, and nothing afterwards can repair it, because reaching it would need the credential it no longer accepts. So a node that is merely switched off stops the rotation and gets named.

The dialog shows the four passes, the nodes that will be written and what this cannot promise, and it wants the cluster's name typed — checked again on the server, so a client that skipped the box gets nothing. The same thing from the command line: holzkubectl rotate-authority prints the plan and does nothing until --confirm names the cluster.

What it does not promise: that your cluster survives it. Every pass is measured against the simulator, which learned for this to adopt a configuration it is given and to derive its own TLS from it. Nobody has run this against real hardware. The dialog says so before you type anything, and the Kubernetes authority is deliberately not touched.

Thirty controls were still too small for a thumb on a phone, and now none are: the dropdowns on Images, Audit and Settings, the checkboxes whose label is the part being tapped, every extension row on Images, the talosconfig file picker, and the clickable rows in the audit log. The desk keeps its compact sizes.

And the size is measured on every push from now on, not written down once. The layout check already drove every screen at a phone width to find content out of reach; it now also measures every button, link and field against 44 pixels there — reach and being able to hit it are different things, and only the first was ever checked.

The check also waits for a screen to finish loading before measuring it, and says how many controls it looked at. It had been measuring after a fixed delay, so a slow machine measured a half-loaded page — and a page whose data never arrived looked like a clean result.

A node that nobody has asked yet is no longer counted as not answering. Right after an import, and after every restart, the cluster card said "1 not answering" for the few seconds before the first check — about a node that was fine. It now says "not checked yet" until there is an answer, and "not answering" only after checks have actually failed.

A machine whose cluster you forgot is no longer shown as down. It stays in the inventory on purpose, because the hardware still exists, but without a cluster there is nothing to ask it with, and that is not the same as it failing to answer.

Importing tells you which field is wrong. Typing the address of the machine holzkube-manager itself runs on now says exactly that instead of "the node is unreachable", and uploading a machine configuration (controlplane.yaml) into the talosconfig field says which file is meant — and that the one you picked holds the cluster's CA key.

The same cluster can no longer be adopted twice. It could, and it did more than duplicate: nodes are filed by their machine id, so the second adoption quietly took the node away from the first cluster, which was left showing something no heartbeat could ever confirm. An adoption through a node another cluster already has is now refused, and the message names the cluster to forget first.

A sign-in or confirmation that comes back from the identity provider and is refused before anything is checked with it now says why in the journal. The last attempt to delete a cluster here came back, was sent to the sign-in page within 32 microseconds, and left not one line — so for three days the wrong cause was assumed. The journal now names the check, says whether the session was still there, and never records the one-time values themselves.
A confirmation that succeeds through the identity provider is logged with how fresh the provider says the sign-in was, so whether it sends that at all is finally something the journal can answer.

A node that was up no longer reads as not answering. Every heartbeat refused its own reads before they left the process — a Talos call without a deadline is refused by design, and the background observer never gave its calls one. After two such passes the node was marked down and its live watch was torn down and rebuilt, every forty-five seconds, for as long as the daemon ran. The request to refresh a node by hand carried a deadline, which is why that one looked fine. Found in the journal of the Raspberry Pi this runs on, not by a test: every test started the observer with a deadline and so supplied exactly what production lacked. A guard now starts it the way the daemon does.

Waiting says what it is doing, for how long, and how long that usually takes. A running job shows its elapsed time next to its steps and an expected duration measured from jobs of the same kind that actually succeeded — the median, so one run that waited an hour on a person does not move it for ever. Image builds keep their last real waits in this browser and say plainly when there is no experience yet. The server's time limit stays visible and is labelled as the moment it gives up, never as a prediction.
A disabled button says why beside it rather than only in a tooltip, because a phone has no hover.

The interface fits a phone. The sidebar was 224px of a 390px screen — 57% of it — and below it the content had 118px left. The page never scrolled sideways, so nothing announced this; it just looked cramped, and where cramped ran out the content simply left. Twenty-two controls were clipped with no way to reach them, seventeen on Settings alone, including the whole "New account" form and the button that changes a password.

Below a tablet width the navigation is now a drawer: a button in the header opens it, the backdrop and following a link close it. Above that width nothing changes at all — the desk layout was not the problem. Measured again afterwards over the same ten screens: nothing out of reach, and the usable width went from 118 to 358 pixels.

Controls are sized for a thumb on a phone. Not one reached 44px before — the standard was 32 to 36 — and now sixty-two do, while the desk keeps the compact sizes, because a list of rows loses real information when every row grows twelve pixels.

A table that scrolls sideways says so. These are 574 and 855 pixels wide on a phone and were fully reachable by swiping, with nothing indicating it — and a cut edge with no scrollbar looks exactly like content that has been cut off for good. It now carries a shade on the right that appears only while there is more, and it can be scrolled with a keyboard.

And a guard holds it. Every push starts the product, signs in, and drives every screen at a phone width and a desk width, failing if anything ends up out of reach. It is part of the chain rather than something to remember to run: this project already has two ledger entries about a watcher that existed and was never scheduled.

A refused confirmation now says which refusal it was, and who fixes it. Confirming a destructive action through an identity provider means proving it asked you again just now, and the only proof is the auth_time claim — which is OPTIONAL in OIDC. A provider that does not send it makes this permanently impassable, however often you try, and that read exactly like a provider that merely declined to re-prompt. The two are told apart now: one is the provider's claim configuration, the other is signing out there first.

And you are no longer left on a page of raw JSON. A problem document reached by navigation renders in the address bar — the sign-in flow was fixed for that long ago and the confirmation flow had been deliberately left out, on the correct grounds that the sign-in page is the wrong destination for somebody already signed in. Correct, and no more readable. It now comes back into the application with an explanation.

Both refusals write a line naming the issuer, the auth_time received, how old it was, and the remedy. The server knew all of this and wrote none of it down — the same gap, one day and one subsystem apart.

Coming back from your identity provider no longer loses what you were doing in silence. The trip is a full page navigation, so the request waiting behind the confirmation cannot survive it — correctly, since nothing was confirmed yet. But nothing said so, and an action still sitting there undone is indistinguishable from one that failed. A banner now names what you started, states plainly that it did not run, and takes you back to the screen you started it on.

What is remembered is the intent and never the request. Replaying the original request across a page navigation would mean keeping it in browser storage — and for the password change, which is gated the same way, that would be the password. Only the sentence and the screen are kept, for ten minutes, and a test pins that shape against a future change that wants to be more helpful.

If you sign in through an identity provider, destructive actions are possible again. The confirmation dialog only ever offered a password field — and an account that signs in through a provider has no local password, while a host declared SSO-only refuses the password routes outright. Every destructive action in the product sat behind a form that could not be filled in, showing a refusal that reads like a mistake.

The dialog now sends you to your provider instead. That route existed the whole time and is careful: it asks the provider to authenticate you afresh, checks on the way back that it really did rather than reusing a session, and that the identity returning is the one signed in. Nothing in the interface offered it. The action you were attempting is not carried across the round trip — run it again when you return, and it will not ask twice.

Third time in two days that a route existed with nothing calling it, and the first that locked an operator out entirely. The new use guard could not see this one either: it checks functions that SEND a request, and a path the browser NAVIGATES to is never sent. It now checks those too.

The phantom node is gone. Adoption read a Talos membership entry — which is named after the node's HOSTNAME, not its UUID — and filed that string as a machine id. The check meant to skip the node it had already recorded compared a hostname against a UUID and was never once true, so your control plane was recorded twice: correctly under its UUID, and again under its hostname at whichever address the membership happened to list first. The second record could never answer, because no certificate is minted for that identity.

Every member is now asked who it is, at each address it reports, in order — the same thing "add a node by address" does with an address you type. It is filed under the UUID it answers with, at the address that answered. That also settles which address gets recorded, which used to be left to the order the cluster happened to report them in.

A member that answers at none of its addresses gets no record and a warning naming it and every address tried. The inventory can now be missing a machine the cluster knows about, and that is the deliberate trade: a record under a key nothing can reach is the phantom above, and it looks adopted.

The same confusion decided the ROLE of a machine added by address: control-plane nodes were filed as workers, and a worker is left out of the etcd reads only control-plane nodes get. Invisible until now, because nothing in the interface could reach that function at all.

When a node does not answer, the journal now says what came back and at which address. It knew all along — the reason is classified and shown per field on the screen — and wrote none of it down, so a real cluster's journal held "the node stopped answering" every interval for hours and nothing else. The address is there because a record can be filed against an address its machine does not answer at, and without it that is indistinguishable from a machine that is switched off.

It says it twice and then stops: once on the first failure, once when the count crosses into down. A node that is down stays down and is asked again every interval, so logging each attempt is the other way to make a journal useless. The raw error goes to the log and the classified sentence to the screen — a gRPC status string in a dashboard cell pushes the actionable part off the edge.

A cluster can be removed again. The route and the API client both had it; nothing on any screen called them, so an imported cluster could not be taken back out. Forgetting removes this installation's record and the secrets derived from it — the cluster itself is untouched, and its machines stay in the inventory without a cluster, because they are machines that still exist.

A node can be added by address. Adoption fills the inventory from the membership the adopted node reports, and records each member under the FIRST address it reports — so a machine reachable at some other address had no way in. The code called this "the always-available second way into the inventory"; it was neither available nor a way.

The guard that exists to stop exactly this was green over both. It reads the whole web interface as one text and asks whether a route's path appears in it — and the API client is part of that text, so a client function nothing calls satisfied it. It now asks the second question separately: does any screen call the client function that issues this route? It found these two on its own.

A cluster you import is now actually watched. Adoption recorded every node it found and asked nobody to look at any of them, so a freshly imported cluster read "not answering" for every machine — including the control plane the import had just authenticated to, because adoption proves it can reach that node before it stores anything. The health column was telling you nothing was there, about a node it had just spoken to.

It took a restart to fix itself, and that is why this looked intermittent. Observers were started for whatever was on disk when the daemon came up, so a cluster imported afterwards stayed invisible until the next restart happened to pick it up. Now a machine gets its observer at the moment it enters the inventory, which is the one place that cannot be forgotten.

The guard for this existed and was aimed one step to the left: it proved that the observer a handler starts outlives the request that started it, after an earlier bug ended them early. Nobody asked whether the import path started one at all. The new test reproduces the operator's own order — daemon running, cluster imported after — and checks the screen rather than the internals.

Three drift guards that compare the web interface against the server no longer accept a renamed leftover. Each matched a name wherever it appeared in the text, so a constant renamed by appending to it — REFUSED_RANGES_LEGACY, or a warning code gaining a suffix — kept them green over exactly the drift they exist to catch. What they still cannot see is now written down and measured, one entry per mechanism, instead of claimed to be nothing.

Built against Talos machinery v1.14, which is what a current cluster actually serves. The previous builds advertised support up to v1.14 while pinning the v1.13.9 library — so this product claimed a Talos whose configuration documents its own library could not read, and the first real cluster it was pointed at failed on exactly that.

A machine configuration is read whole again. v1.16.2 selected the v1alpha1 document and ignored the rest, reasoning that every secret lives in it. That was true of Talos v1.13 and is false of v1.14, where the Kubernetes API-server CA is a document of its own — so that approach would have derived a bundle with the Kubernetes CA missing and refused a control-plane node as a worker. Confidently wrong, which is worse than the error it replaced.

A configuration document this build does not know is now a refusal that names it, says which Talos versions this build was made for, and gives the remedy: upgrade holzkube-manager. Not an Internal error, and not a bundle derived from the parts that happened to be recognised — an unknown document can be the one carrying a secret.

Adoption cannot crash the daemon on a configuration it is handed. machinery v1.14 dereferences five accessors without checking them, so a worker's configuration — which has no API-server CA — panics rather than returning an empty bundle as v1.13 did. The configuration is now asked what kind of node it is before anything is derived, and all five are checked first.

Two new guards keep the pin honest, because the operator updates Talos as soon as a release lands. One runs in the build and refuses a supported range wider than the compiled-in machinery can read; the other asks weekly whether a newer stable machinery exists and fails when one does — scheduled rather than opt-in, because this project already has a drift watcher nobody scheduled.

Adopting a real cluster works. It did not: the first real Talos cluster this product was ever pointed at refused adoption with "Internal error", and the reason was a document adoption does not read. A Talos machine configuration is multi-document YAML — one v1alpha1 document carrying the secrets, and beside it a growing set of typed documents. machinery decodes a typed document only if this build knows its kind, its loader is all-or-nothing, and there is no option to tolerate one. A DiscoveryServiceConfig document, which machinery v1.13.9 does not have at all, therefore failed the whole parse. Every secret adoption needs is in the v1alpha1 document; not one sibling is read.

The machine configuration document is now selected rather than the whole file parsed, using machinery's own discriminator: the document with version v1alpha1 and no kind. Selecting rather than tolerating is what makes this hold for the next document kind Talos ships — tolerating would leave adoption depending on which unknown documents a node happens to carry, and a manager that must know every kind Talos will ever ship is one that breaks on every Talos release.

A node serving no machine configuration document at all is now refused as the wrong node — a 400 that names the remedy — instead of failing to parse and arriving as an Internal error nobody can act on.

An Internal error now names the request, so the line that explains it can be found in the server log. That family strips its detail on purpose — the underlying text can name a path, a hostname or the contents of a configuration — which leaves the operator with a true and unusable sentence. The id was already in the response and in the matching log line; only the rendering was missing. Finding this one took a person reading fifty journal lines and sending them on.

The simulator could never have caught this: it serves a configuration the same machinery generated, so by construction every document in it is one this build knows. The test fixture is now the simulator's own config with the operator's document appended — real secrets, real refusal — and it checks that the old path still fails before checking that the new one works, so a machinery that learns the kind will say so rather than quietly proving nothing.

The release you are running is marked as such again. A released build reports its version without a leading v — goreleaser stamps the tag with the v stripped — while this changelog spells versions exactly as the git tag does, so the two never matched and v1.16.0 marked nothing as "running here". The panel normalises instead of insisting, because neither side can simply adopt the other's spelling: the update script compares the tag with its v stripped against what the binary reports, so a binary carrying the v would look out of date on every run and reinstall itself forever.

Found by downloading v1.16.0 and running it, not by a test. Every test passed the version in the changelog's own spelling, and the browser check used a development build — which reports something like v1.16.0-4-gabc-dirty and matches no release at all, so the case that was broken looked exactly like the case that is supposed to match nothing.

The version this instance is running is now on screen, at the bottom of the sidebar, and clicking it opens this list. Until now the only way to find out which build a host was running was to ssh in and ask the binary, which meant nobody asked.
The first release of milestone v1.16 that is not a beta. Everything in the betas below is in it; nothing has been added but the version display.

One thing this release does NOT have, said plainly because the word stable does not say it: holzkube-manager has still never run on real amd64 hardware. Every operation below is proven against the Talos simulator and against a real Image Factory, and the single run that would close OPS-05 — a blank machine becoming a node through the wizard, taking a configuration, being upgraded — has not happened. Two constants remain estimates until it does: how long a machine may take to reappear after provisioning, and after an upgrade. Both are reported against elapsed time rather than enforced as timeouts, so a wrong number costs a misleading sentence and not a failed operation.

The update script would have tossed a coin over which archive to install. It took the first release asset whose name ended in linux_<arch>.tar.gz, and since holzkubectl got an archive of its own there are two of those. It now names the prefix that tells them apart, and more than one match is refused rather than resolved by luck.

A release is published rather than left as a draft, and a beta is deliberately not marked as a prerelease: the endpoint the update script reads skips both, so marking a beta as a prerelease would leave every host on the previous build while reporting itself up to date.

The release pipeline checks the release an operator would actually download — both Linux architectures present, exactly one daemon archive each, checksums there, and visible to the update script — because the build reporting success only means it uploaded what it built.

Removing a node from a cluster asks etcd first. Until now it did not read the membership at all: the refusal existed, on a different function, and the button went straight to leaving the cluster and then wiped the disk. The refusal was also wrong — it let the last voting member go. A majority of n is n/2+1, so four voting members tolerate exactly as many failures as three; four feels safer and is not.
Scaling a cluster is one view rather than two operations on nodes: what this cluster can spare, what adding or removing would mean, and why. It reaches etcd only when asked.
etcd can be restored from a snapshot, not only backed up. The README used to say so in the other direction: a backup that cannot be restored is a file, not a recovery.
kubeconfig without going through talosctl — the tool this product exists to replace.

Users, roles and service accounts. Machine labels, machine classes and cluster templates. A command-line client, holzkubectl, which is a client of this same API and not a second implementation of anything.

Disk encryption at install, with the node's own ID or its TPM. A static key is refused because for the STATE volume it ends up in plaintext in META, and a key server is refused because a node whose key server is gone does not boot — which reverses the decision this product stands on.

The installer image is resolved against the Image Factory instead of being assembled from parts. The old string was wrong three ways at once, each silently: it never carried SecureBoot, so a machine booted from a SecureBoot image installed a system that was not; it hardcoded one repository name; and it hardcoded the public Factory, so an installation pointed at a private one provisioned nodes that pulled from the public one.

The certificate countdown has a door: this installation's own client certificate can be renewed from the screen that warns about it. The new certificate is proved against a node before it replaces the one in use, so a failure changes nothing.
A node that answers but cannot be read is no longer indistinguishable from one that is absent. The two lead to different repairs — the cable or the power supply, against the node itself.

The first public release: the store and its forward-only migrations, the hash-chained audit log, authentication with a re-authentication window for destructive actions, the Talos transport seam with a deadline class per call, and the Image Factory screen.
